body:
Understanding noncommunicable diseases

Noncommunicable diseases, commonly called NCDs, are diseases that do not spread from one person to another as infectious diseases do. Many NCDs last for years and require continuing prevention, monitoring or care.

Their causes are often complex. Genetic factors, ageing, environmental exposures, nutrition and behaviour may act together. An individual can develop an NCD even without an obvious behavioural risk factor.

The 4 major groups of NCDs

GroupExamplesImportant concept
Cardiovascular diseasesCoronary heart disease, heart attack, strokeDisorders affecting the heart or blood vessels
CancersLung, breast, oral and cervical cancersAbnormal uncontrolled growth of cells
Chronic respiratory diseasesAsthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary diseaseLong-term disorders affecting breathing and the airways
DiabetesType 1 and type 2 diabetesDisturbed regulation of blood glucose

Cardiovascular diseases affect the heart and blood vessels. A heart attack generally results from interrupted blood flow to part of the heart muscle. A stroke occurs when blood supply to part of the brain is interrupted or bleeding damages brain tissue.

Cancer involves abnormal, uncontrolled cell growth. Some cancers can spread to other organs. Not all abnormal growths are cancerous, and cancer itself is not transmitted by ordinary contact.

Asthma involves inflammation and variable narrowing of the airways. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is associated with persistent airflow limitation and is strongly linked with exposure to tobacco smoke and other harmful particles.

Diabetes mellitus involves persistently elevated blood glucose. Type 1 diabetes usually results from autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing cells. Type 2 diabetes commonly involves reduced responsiveness to insulin together with inadequate insulin production for the body's needs. The causes of these 2 forms are not identical.

Behavioural, metabolic and environmental risk factors

Risk factors are conditions that increase the probability of disease. They are not proof that a particular person has a disease.

  • Behavioural risks: Tobacco use, unhealthy diet, insufficient physical activity and harmful alcohol consumption.
  • Metabolic risks: Elevated blood pressure, high blood glucose, abnormal blood lipids and overweight or obesity.
  • Environmental risks: Air pollution and exposure to harmful substances.
  • Non-modifiable risks: Age and inherited susceptibility.

For example, a high-salt diet may contribute to elevated blood pressure, which increases the risk of stroke and heart disease. However, high blood pressure can also occur for reasons not directly explained by salt intake.

Nutritional deficiency diseases

Deficiency diseases occur when the body does not receive or adequately use an essential nutrient. They are non-infectious, even though infections and poor nutrition may sometimes occur together.

DeficiencyAssociated conditionCharacteristic effect
IronIron deficiency anaemiaReduced haemoglobin production
Vitamin ANight blindnessDifficulty seeing in dim light
Vitamin CScurvyBleeding gums and impaired connective tissue maintenance
Vitamin DRickets in childrenImpaired bone mineralisation
IodineIodine deficiency disorders, including goitreDisturbed thyroid hormone production

Preventing and detecting NCDs

Healthy eating, physical activity, avoiding tobacco, reducing harmful alcohol use and limiting exposure to air pollution can reduce important risks. Screening can identify people who need further assessment for conditions such as hypertension, diabetes or certain cancers.

Screening is not the same as a confirmed diagnosis. An abnormal screening result may require additional evaluation by a qualified healthcare professional.

Some infectious agents increase the risk of particular cancers. Persistent infection with certain high-risk types of human papillomavirus can lead to cervical cancer. This does not make cervical cancer itself a contagious disease.

Prelims focus

  • The 4 major NCD groups are cardiovascular diseases, cancers, chronic respiratory diseases and diabetes.
  • Tobacco use and physical inactivity are behavioural risk factors.
  • Elevated blood pressure and blood glucose are metabolic risk factors.
  • Scurvy results from vitamin C deficiency; rickets can result from vitamin D deficiency.
  • Persistent high-risk HPV infection is an important cause of cervical cancer.
  • Trap: A risk factor increases probability; it is not the same as a confirmed diagnosis.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 13, Why Do We Fall Ill?, section 13.2; WHO, Noncommunicable Diseases, fact sheet dated 25 September 2025; WHO, Cardiovascular Diseases, fact sheet dated 31 July 2025; WHO, Diabetes, fact sheet dated 14 November 2024; WHO, Cervical Cancer, fact sheet dated 3 July 2026; online sources consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Noncommunicable Diseases, Nutritional Deficiencies and Risk Factors

body:
Adolescence and puberty are different concepts

Adolescence is the developmental period between childhood and adulthood. The World Health Organization defines adolescents as people aged 10–19 years.

This period includes physical growth, emotional changes, increasing independence, cognitive development and social adjustment.

Puberty is the biological process through which the reproductive organs mature and secondary sexual characteristics develop. Puberty overlaps with adolescence and can begin earlier, but adolescence includes much more than reproductive maturation.

Primary sexual characteristics are reproductive organs directly involved in reproduction. Secondary sexual characteristics are physical features that develop during puberty but are not directly involved in reproduction.

Changes during puberty

Puberty involves an increase in hormonal activity. Signals from the brain and pituitary gland stimulate the testes or ovaries, which produce sex hormones and support reproductive maturation.

  • Common changes: Rapid increase in height, growth of pubic and underarm hair, changes in body composition, increased sweating and sometimes acne.
  • Common changes in boys: Enlargement of the testes and penis, beginning of sperm production, deepening of the voice and increased facial hair.
  • Common changes in girls: Breast development, maturation of the ovaries and uterus, and eventual onset of menstruation.
  • Emotional and social changes: Greater self-awareness, developing independence and changing relationships with peers and family.

The age at which these changes occur varies considerably. A difference in timing between adolescents does not, by itself, establish that development is abnormal.

Reproductive hormones

The pituitary gland releases follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinising hormone (LH). These hormones help regulate the reproductive organs.

In the testes, hormonal signals support sperm production and testosterone secretion. In the ovaries, FSH and LH help regulate follicle development, ovulation and hormone secretion.

Oestrogen contributes to female secondary sexual characteristics and growth of the uterine lining. Progesterone helps prepare and maintain the uterine lining for possible pregnancy.

The menstrual cycle

The menstrual cycle is a repeating sequence of hormonal and reproductive changes. In adults, a cycle commonly lasts about 21–35 days, although normal variation exists. Cycles can be irregular during the first years after menstruation begins.

Main events

  1. Menstruation: The uterine lining is shed as menstrual bleeding when pregnancy has not occurred and the relevant hormone levels fall.
  2. Follicular development: A follicle develops in the ovary while the uterine lining begins to thicken again.
  3. Ovulation: A mature egg is released from an ovary. A rise in LH is an important trigger.
  4. Luteal phase: The corpus luteum formed after ovulation releases progesterone, helping maintain the uterine lining. If pregnancy does not begin, hormone levels fall and another period follows.

The first menstrual period is called menarche. The permanent natural cessation of menstrual cycles later in life is called menopause.

Ovulation does not always occur on day 14. The day of ovulation varies with cycle length and individual circumstances. A calendar estimate alone cannot reliably establish whether pregnancy is possible.

Menstrual health and adolescent well-being

Good menstrual health includes accurate information, access to clean menstrual products, water, sanitation, privacy and appropriate healthcare. Menstruation is a normal physiological process, not an illness.

Adolescents also benefit from adequate nutrition, regular physical activity, sufficient sleep, emotional support and reliable information about reproductive health. Persistent severe menstrual pain, very heavy bleeding or other concerning symptoms should be assessed by a healthcare professional rather than assumed to be normal.

Prelims focus

  • WHO defines adolescence as ages 10–19 years.
  • Puberty concerns biological sexual maturation; adolescence also includes psychological and social development.
  • FSH and LH are pituitary hormones involved in reproductive regulation.
  • The LH surge is an important trigger for ovulation.
  • Menarche is the first menstrual period; menopause is the permanent natural end of menstrual cycles.
  • Trap: Ovulation is not fixed on day 14 in every menstrual cycle.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 10, Reaching the Age of Adolescence, sections 10.1–10.6; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 3, Human Reproduction, sections on gametogenesis and menstrual cycle; WHO, Adolescent Health, overview; WHO, Menstrual Health, fact sheet dated 18 June 2026; online sources consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Adolescence, Puberty and the Menstrual Cycle

body:
Human sexual reproduction

Human reproduction involves the formation of male and female gametes, their fusion during fertilisation and subsequent development of an embryo.

Gametes are reproductive cells containing one set of chromosomes. In humans, a typical sperm and a typical egg each contain 23 chromosomes. Their fusion usually restores the diploid number of 46 chromosomes in the zygote.

Male reproductive system

The testes produce sperm cells and secrete testosterone. Sperm develop and mature through the male reproductive tract and are transported through ducts. Accessory glands contribute fluids to semen, which carries sperm.

Sperm production begins at puberty. The testes normally lie in the scrotum, where conditions support sperm development.

Female reproductive system

The ovaries contain developing egg cells and secrete hormones, including oestrogen and progesterone. The fallopian tubes, also called oviducts, help transport the released egg. The uterus supports implantation and development during pregnancy. The cervix forms the lower part of the uterus, connecting it with the vagina.

Usually, one egg is released during an ovulatory menstrual cycle, although more than one egg may sometimes be released.

Fertilisation, implantation and development

  1. Ovulation: The ovary releases an egg.
  2. Fertilisation: A sperm fuses with the egg, usually in a fallopian tube, forming a zygote.
  3. Early division: The zygote undergoes repeated cell divisions while moving towards the uterus.
  4. Implantation: The developing blastocyst attaches to and embeds in the uterine lining.
  5. Embryonic development: Cells differentiate and major body structures begin to form.
  6. Foetal development: Growth and maturation continue through the remainder of pregnancy.

Fertilisation is the fusion of gametes. Implantation is the attachment and embedding of the developing embryo in the uterine lining. They are different events occurring at different locations.

The placenta and pregnancy

The placenta is an organ that develops during pregnancy and allows the exchange of oxygen, nutrients and metabolic wastes between maternal and foetal circulations. Maternal and foetal blood generally remain in separate circulatory systems while exchange occurs across the placental barrier.

Human pregnancy is commonly dated from the first day of the last menstrual period and lasts about 40 weeks on that basis, although actual delivery time varies.

Antenatal care includes monitoring maternal health and foetal growth, providing nutritional advice, identifying risks and arranging appropriate healthcare. Iron and folic-acid supplementation, when recommended through antenatal services, helps address important maternal nutritional needs.

Sex chromosomes and the sex of a child

In the usual XX/XY pattern of sex-chromosome inheritance, an egg contributes an X chromosome. A sperm contributes either an X or a Y chromosome. Fertilisation by an X-bearing sperm ordinarily produces an XX combination, while fertilisation by a Y-bearing sperm ordinarily produces an XY combination.

Biological sex development is more complex in some individuals because chromosomal and developmental variations occur. Nevertheless, in the standard school-level genetic model, the sperm determines whether the typical combination is XX or XY. The mother is not responsible for choosing the sex of a child.

Health across pregnancy and early life

Safe pregnancy and childbirth require more than the absence of a diagnosed illness. Good nutrition, timely antenatal check-ups, skilled care during delivery, postnatal care, breastfeeding support and newborn immunisation all contribute to maternal and child health.

Prelims focus

  • Typical human gametes contain 23 chromosomes; the zygote contains 46.
  • Testes produce sperm; ovaries produce female gametes.
  • Fertilisation usually occurs in a fallopian tube.
  • Implantation occurs in the uterine lining.
  • The placenta enables exchange between maternal and foetal circulations.
  • Trap: Fertilisation and implantation are not the same process.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 9, Reproduction in Animals, sections 9.1–9.2; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 3, Human Reproduction, sections 3.1–3.7; National Health Mission, Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, Adolescent Health and Nutrition framework, consulted 3 November 2026.]
